The F2A fits into your BURN2 via the pins that stick straight out. On the face of it is a small connector- that is where the F2E cable connects if you use one. Your F3 chipset slips onto the connector on the edge of your F2A to be burnt- you'll notice the edge connector looks suspiciously like your J3 port on your ecm. However I'm not aware that Load or Load% are used to decide how much fuel is used OTHER than as inputs to fuel tables. The EEC uses airmass times an assumed Air-to-fuel ratio value to calculate fuel mass. That air-to-fuel multiplier is what's being manipulated when you adjust the Z_AFR scalar in the GUFx tunes. This might beg the question of what the EEC is doing with the value in the fuel table. It's using it as a multiplier. The Air-to-Fuel multiplier (aka Z_AFR) is a stoic conversion. However if you need a rich mix of say 11:1 instead of 14.64, then you command 11:1 in the fuel table. In the case of FN1360, 11 will be at the top row for all RPMs. To the EEC, that 11 value is in terms of lambda which is ~.75. response: I have a '97 F-350 with a 7.3L Powerstroke Turbo Diesel, I frequently haul a 27ft bumper tow trailer weighing upwards of 6,000 lbs, which by the way it tows beautifully, but if i am pulling up a long hill or have been on the pedal for a while and let off, then there is a grinding sound that sounds like it is coming from the turbo. My dad and i think it may be some sort of exhaust overflow valve from the quick decrease in rpm or maybe an overspeed on the turbo. No noticeable decrease in power. Anyone have any ideas or experienced the same thing? It very well may be your turbo or the turbo dump valve. WHen you let off throttle after being on it (and under boost) for a while when you let off the pedal the turbo system is supposed to “dump” the high pressure so that it doesnt slam shut the throttle valve…if i had boost in the system when you let off the pedal the pressure will slam into the closing throttle door. YOu may not be properly venting this pressure out via the dump valve this will also cause the pressure wave to back up into the turbo…damaging the compressor wheel…making it slam into the body of the turbo. Your realistic options would be to find out for sure if there is a def file for your EEC or replace the EEC with one that does have a def file and will work with your setup. But realistically, disassembling the BIN and making your own definition isn't likely an option. While it is true that this can be done and indeed is how others make def files, they don't have an automated program that does all this for them. There's a significant amount of work just to get a clean disassembly. Then once they have that, they have to make heads-or-tails of the code, identify the meaningful pieces, and make a def file that points to them, associate English names and descriptions to them, and convert them from their computer-centric values to units that mean something to humans (e.g. kg/hr, lb/m, seconds, degrees advance, etc). instruction: Explain ignition timing in ECU tuning
response: I am fairly new to the scooby crowd, but have been around turbos and AWD for quite some time now and am a little confused. After reading some threads for a while, I can't believe some of the questions and advice being thrown around. Some TFoz guy asked if he needed to retune his car after adding an exhaust system and the response was based on what kind of exhaust he was running. The car is stock! Unless the factory wasegate system is not up to the task of limiting boost, there is now way an OEM ECU would allow any damage to the car. At worst, it might pull timing if the intake air is really hot or the MAS sees airflow beyond stock limitations. What happened to using a wideband O2 sensor, knock values and a datalogger? Shoot, 2G DSM guys can't even see knock on the ECU, yet they tune monsters simply by watching the timing advance curve vs RPM. Also, what is with scooby guys using 20+ year old turbo compressors and outdated MHI crap. Look at the EvoIII 16G map compared to the old 18G...the 18G is very inefficient in a TDO5H housing and flows the same. I guess there are a bunch of little things I just don't understand about the mainstream scooby upgrades.

Your cam has overlap for sure since mine at 220/220 has only 7 degrees of negative overlap (no overlap). With that cam your going to have to give the motor what it wants not what looks good on paper. Your iscduty cycle was at 49% average and it should be around 35%. Logging your vacuum/boost would be very helpful in perfecting the idle, bottom line make a fuel change, run a log and go look at the vacuum in the log, import it into a microsoft excel program and average your vacuum and rpm. Its only for safety concerns you add more fuel to reduce the chances of detonation. The higher the octane fuel you burn the leaner you can run the engine due to the safety provided by the fuel, this doesnt apply to alcohol im referring to gasoline only. Typically with higher octane fuels 108+ you can run boosted engines at the leanest AFR that they are efficient at. now alcohol and ethanol are much different, alcohol responds similar to diesel, the more u inject the more power they make, but like everything in life there is a point of diminishing returns i tend to run an engine as rich as it responds to, what i mean by that is if i run an engine at .9 lambda and drop it to .85 lambda and it doesnt decrease acceleration rate then i leave that fuel in with fuel a dyno is about useless, dynos measure twisting force TORQUE "most" dont factor in acceleration rate, fuel usually doesnt effect the RWHP that much its more prodominate when measuring acceler...

instruction: Explain MAF tuning in ECU tuning
response: For anyone who has ever installed an aftermarket turbocharger system on a naturally aspirated car, upgraded the turbos and/or fuel system on a turbocharged car, or wanted to remove the restrictive MAF meter on any car, the MAP ECU (Manifold Absolute Pressure Electronic Control Unit) is for you! This piggy-back system is similar in function and design to the super-popular HKS VPC (now discontinued) however, the MAP ECU takes it one step further by allowing end-user programmability via Windows-based software. The purpose of the MAP ECU is to mimic the voltage or frequency output patterns of the factory Mass Air Flow(hotwire) or Karman-Vortex meter but uses RPM and Manifold Pressure to make its calculations rather than airflow. Basic setup takes only a few minutes, and allows the user to custom tailor the MAP ECU to work with almost any automotive system on the planet. The user can set the number of cylinders (1-16), type of air metering system utilized (Karman-Vortex or Hotwire), throttle position hi/low voltage range, throttle or MAP based enrichment, and the type of oxygen sensor utilized (OEM or wideband). Although depending on how you leave the tune setup, there may only be 1 place you NEED to go. The EASY way is to go to the WOT Spark Function and reduce all those values by 10. At non-WOT conditions, you probably don't need a retard of 10°. However to be safe, you might also go to each of the 3 spark tables (Sealevel, Alt, and Base) and reduce the top row by 10° just to make sure all high-load conditions get the retard you are looking for. Again that's the quick-n-dirty way. But not the best way. IMO, the best way to handle a boosted application using a GUFx EEC like the X3Z is to disable the WOT Spark Functions. WOT Spark functions are RPM-based only. They don't allow you to take into account Load. On naturally aspirated engines, that's not a big deal. When E85 became very popular in the corn states, mfgs got nervous and decided they had to make the engines, at least, tolerant of accidentally being fed E85 or purposefully fed E85 in some misguided sense of state-patriotism. And when E15 was approved by the EPA for 2001-newer vehicles, that just furthered this effort of being E85-tolerant even if not E85 optimized the way an official FFV would be. Another possibility that might explain your issue is you have something mechanical that you haven't found yet. Something as simple as a clogged PCV valve will alter things enough to throw idle stability a little. Depending on how much blow-by the engine experiences, the tune could be inadvertently expecting the unburned fuel in the blow-by as part of the intake fuel supply at idle loads and with a clogged PCV, it's not getting it and the injectors are having to make up the difference. Again, I don't know if it'd be 15% difference, but it's just something to check or think about. It's also worth note that a sticky PCV is more detrimental to idle stability than a stuck-solid valve. Turbodnotch wrote: ...I have the spec sheet that came with my Pro-M MAF, are those the values I would enter into the MAF transfer function table and fine tune from there? If the values are in terms of kg/hr, then yes. Although many MAF mfgs only give you a 9pt MAF Curve. You'll need to use EEC Analyzer (or some other utility) to extrapolate out a 30pt curve from the 9pt curve to give you more accuracy and control of the MAF. The 30pt version will be what you put into the tune...and the curve needs to be in terms of kg/hr, not lb/min. Turbodnotch wrote: ...Do I rescale my load parameters to account for the timing required while in boost situations? Most definitely. response: AFM powerpipe G-FORCE T-5 and 3.55 gears Top Blackarma Regular Posts: 73 Joined: Mon Apr 21, 2014 12:20 am Re: How much to add to MAF transfer based on Lambse/WB delta Quote Post by Blackarma » Thu May 15, 2014 7:24 pm Datalog your maf, maf voltage and wb readings. Take a maf voltage reading, in your logs, that matches closely to the voltage in the transfer curve. See what your afr is reading at that voltage. Divide your afr read you logged by stoich. Then take your answer and multiply it by the air flow reading in your curve by the same maf voltage. You will want to start with the readings at idle and work from there. If your number is <1.0 then it will lean when you multiply, >1.0 then it will richen when you multiply. It's not too big a deal if it's below the drivability threshold. 2) transient fuel, not accel fuel, is designed to minimize the negative overshoot after an accel by setting the AFR close to stoich on a gradually decaying slope (until the min threshold (TFCDED) is hit.) This is done specifically to combat the CL desire to quickly bring the mixture back to stoich (causing an overshoot). I know this concept is more difficult for the average tuner to grasp, but it is very powerful when understood and properly implemented as I have discovered. I spent over a year fighting the lean at/after tip-in bug - now I have no issue at all. response: of idle (the above functions), into drive (the spark tables) doesn't give me a jolt as the spark advance transitions. Keeping these functions and the tables close in value has improved the transition dramatically. It used to be I would almost refuse to drive-idle the truck because I hated having to transition by pressing the throttle. EVERY TIME it would jerk and buck in 1st gear when I ever-so-slightly moved the throttle because the idle timing was around 18 and my tables were still at default 28. That's a 10 degree jump...and that's going to create a power differential. And when it happens suddenly with the truck in 1st gear, it was down right annoying. But now, I can press the throttle with no jerks or rough transitions at all. If I press lightly, I get a smooth acceleration and spark doesn't change more than about 2-3 degrees between idle (~19-20°) and drive (~22°). The increase of 2 degrees is probably a good thing as load is increasing. But not 10°... The only negative part to this is the engine is capable of producing much more torque for the fuel being used. Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Jan 19, 2010 11:54 am Transient does pull fuel. But the time it takes for it to come and go should be shorter than a typical HEGO switch. So long decels should not have an ongoing transient leanout. Keep in mind that transient enrichment only happens on Change in Load. When the Load goes from 20% to 50%, there's a positive enrichment over a short period of time. When the load drops from 50% to 20%, there's a negative enrichment (what I'm calling enleanment if that's a real word) over a short period of time. But once the decel is sustained, the load should be fairly stable. Depending on the vehicle, a high RPM Closed Throttle Decel should be in the low teens at the highest. My engine easily gets into the single digits on decel. You'll see...

response: Wed Jun 02, 2010 11:37 am, edited 1 time in total. -Clint- Top cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: MAF Tuning Question Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Jun 02, 2010 11:36 am When you use a larger injector and run a calibrated MAF, the MAF is compensating for the larger injector by reporting a lower voltage than what the stock MAF would. To the EEC running the stock tune, this means less air is being aspirated into the engine, so the EEC commands a shorter injector pulse. The MAF is trying to reduce the injector pulse by the same amount as the larger injector is over-performing as compared to a stock injector. When you enter the MAF's actual flow curve and actual injector size into your tune, you are no longer relying on the MAF to compensate. The EEC is no longer being lied to. The EEC is aware that a lower voltage is higher flow rate with the updated MAF curve. Likewise, the EEC is also aware of just how large the injectors are so it can calculate fueling as-is...no compensation relied on. Does that help? ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lowe...

instruction: Explain dyno tuning in ECU tuning
response: by the Fuel Cranking Injector PW function. Once the engine turns over on its own power, the EEC should transition over to normal Fueling based on the OL Fuel table (FN1307) and Startup Enrichment Fueling table (FN1306). The few seconds right after crank are often quite rich, but that should bleed off fairly quickly as the combustion chamber warms up. However if the engine begins stalling, the RPMs will drop, ISC will open, both of which means the Load will go up. And as you noticed, as Load goes up, enrichment goes up too. So what needs to be determined is what causes the engine to start dropping in RPMs to start with thus causing the higher load and higher enrichment that probably just exacerbates the problem particularly if over-enrichment is what caused the unintended drop in RPM to start with. So what should you try? Well first, you need to focus in on your datalogs right before the drop in RPM and look for something that could cause this. Things I'd look for are overly rich condition on the WB, too low of spark for the condition, or too much ISC airflow pulled for some reason thus triggering the drop in RPMs. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Ex...

In simpler terms, the Load is the % of air getting into the motor as compared to the theoretical MAX which is the CID (Cubic Inch Displacement). So theoretically, boost should begin when Load = 1 or 100%. If you are finding the EEC is calculating load lower than that but your boost gauges show boost pressures, then that would lead me to believe there's either a problem with the MAF curve, your CID scalar, or some other issue. But I'm also speaking with no experience with a forced induction engine too. response: fueling, because like you, I'm seeing rich tip-outs. I don't trust closed loop fueling to do the right thing here at light loads. I have my tune set up so that low loads (<12%) go open loop, so the mixture then comes from the Base OL fuel table. See LOLOD and LOLODH. Open loop takes over when LOAD < LOLOD - LOLODH, closed loop resumes at LOAD > LOLOD. You might also want to look at how transient fueling handles coming out of DFSO. The stock tunes assume the manifold is still wet, I've found assuming that it's dry works better for my combo. AISFM is the scalar that controls this assumption - 1 is full wet, 0 is full dry. More spark advance means a bigger jerk when fuel kicks in again. Closed throttle spark is controlled by FN111 - beware, this function is used as a baseline for closed loop idle speed spark control! If you make big changes to FN111, you need to change FN841D and FN841N - which are multipliers to FN111 -to restore proper spark timing under closed loop idle. I do not recommend enabling DFSO on shifts, unless you have a very quick gearshift hand! I hope this hasn't been too confusing. It takes some time to sort all this stuff out. '89 LX

instruction: Explain ignition timing in ECU tuning
response: wrote: The answer to the question is to simply adjust the Global Spark adders. In the GUFx defs, there's a spark adder for CT/PT/WOT/Neutral. However what I recommend you do instead of adjusting the scalar adders is adjust the table/function directly. The problem with doing the adder thing is you now have another place that is influencing your spark. Simply going to your spark tables or your WOT Spark function and adding 6-8° is more recommended. In fact to simplify spark even further, you can dumb it right down to 1 table in the GUFx defs by adjusting a few scalars: Disable WOT mode which abandons the WOT functions using Z_WSPKSW Disable the Altitude Spark table using Z_SPKINT Disable the Base Spark table by zeroing out all load cells in FN125 With all that set, you can do most all your spark adjustments out of the Sealevel table only and never look at the other two spark tables. Closed Throttle Idle Spark will still be controlled by the Idle Spark functions. See how that works for you... and also bumped the sealevel timing by 3 degrees across the board. The idle seemed to settle in a little easier, so maybe I will play with that a little more. Eric 1973 Bronco; 393W; 4R70W Auto T...

response: have inconsistent results and the online reviews are often anecdotal and from owners who don't understand the numbers or what's actually occurring when you use one with a car relying on the MAF sensor. So here's my take from a tuner's perspective. My only exception to the rule is when tuning a car on Speed Density, a process by which you no longer rely on the MAF sensor to determine the amount of incoming air. You now rely on pressure and temperature ( MAP sensor + a relocated IAT up to near the throttle / manifold area ) to determine how much air is coming into the engine. That is the only way to avoid the pitfalls that can sometimes occur with a VTA (vent to atmosphere) relief valve. So now the great debate of "why"...... There are multiple reasons but ill try and boil this down for you and make it easy. Most aftermarket BOVs, and yes, even GFB's from my findings, arent entirely air-tight as we think they are. VTA type BOVs act as a vac leak at certain loads. If you arent already aware, ANY air leak after the MAF sensor in a MAF tuned car (excluding SD) is its Achilles heel in the Subaru world. response: One must be very careful about low octane fuel in a forced induction engine because pre-ignition can be death to a turbocharged engine much faster than a normally aspirated one. In the meantime your fuel mileage will probably decline slightly, and the car won’t perform up to its full potential. The manual tells me to use 91 octane or more, but what harm am I doing if I use regular gas? Over the long term using regular can damage the engine. Normally, my opinion is that it depends. The problem with yours is the turbocharger. The only way I would even consider it would be IF there was zero rattling, no drop off in mileage or performance, the EGR system is operational, and a careful examination of a new set of spark plugs after a hundred miles gave it a clean bill of health. It Volvo (owner’s manual) says it is required. Using anything higher is a waste of money, assuming the car is in good condition.

response: I’m curious, why do some cars have live power outlets when the car is running and some do not? Are there advantages or disadvantages of either one that would influence a manufacturer’s decision? I would prefer live at all times, but my 2005 & 2008 Toyota Ravs do not offer that feature. It is simply a choice. People leave things plugged into their power ports. Failures in those things can cause a fire inside the car that owners will try to make warranty claims for. Makes for quite the argument between owners, insurance companies and car companies. Those same devices can drain the battery to the point it won’t start the car. If the port powers down when the key is off none of that can happen. Keep in mind people plug far more than just phone rechargers into these ports. Given the ports usually have 10 amp or larger fuses, that can kill a car battery in about 4 hours. You can re-wire the ports so they stay live at key off if you chose. It isn’t that hard. Thank you for your response, it all makes sense. Sounds like more of an advantage not to keep them live, for sure. Thanks again! Certainly advantageous to the manufacturer! I have one GM vehicle that leaves the power ports live

response: last charge pipe. There are those who have dabbled in putting it into the intake manifold itself, but i have not tried myself, nor do i think its a good idea for getting an accurate representation of air temp. Yes, weather changes DO affect it, but once you have dialed it in for each using just the temp compensation table, you are golden. Result is a perfect AF target that hits no matter the weather. Its not as drastic of an effect as you think, but its enough to need a few tweaks. Absolute best thing you can do besides moving the IAT to the proper place is to get your wideband's analog signal wired to a TGV voltage signal, allowing you to log it, and depending on model, convert it with COBBs custom file to convert itself already. If not, the voltage equation is (TGV voltage signal X 2) + 10 which will take a 0-5 volt signal and translate it into the better known 10 to 20 AFR reading. This will make adjustments for WOT (and anything else) in the SD table SUPER accurate when you lay it all out in a log. response: replaced fuel pump and than check to see and no power Blown fuse, relay or perhaps a damaged power supply wire or faulty connection to pump or bad ground wire/connection. Did you check while cranking and not just with the key in run position. I assume vehicle wont start. Pull a vacuum line off (one from the booster works good) spray some carb cleaner into it (5 sec worth) see if she fires over. Are you sure your checking the right wires at pump? Unless you’re cranking the engine there won’t be any power to the pump. You should also check ALL fuses and this includes the oversized ones in the engine compartment fuse box. If this vehicle uses a variable load control module then one of those larger fuses (40 amp maybe?) also controls the fuel pump through that module. Look at the owners manual for the fuse layout. Power is only applied for the first four seconds the KEY is turned on. Power will not return until the engine STARTS or the key is turned off and back on again. The impact sensor will also disconnect power from the pump.

Start/warmup is the mode immediately after crank where the EEC over-richens while the engine is cold to keep the engine running smooth until the engine is closer to running temps. If you are talking about crank. This one is simple. There's a fairly wide range of acceptable fuel that the EEC could squirt and still get the engine to start. Usually problems here are due to under-fueling. While possible, you usually don't usually flood an engine with EFI without doing something very wrong often hardware related. For instance, leaky injectors could do this. Over-pressured fuel rail delivering way too much fuel. Larger injectors than expected. For start, this one is fairly easy if you have a wideband. First off, you want to be rich. Anything richer than stoic is probably fine but once the engine is running and the mix is rich, fuel the engine to where it idles somewhat smooth. Now this may require a higher idle until the engine warms up a bit in order to get a smooth idle while in start mode. Adam, also make sure to continue to datalog whichever HEGO is next to the WB until you are familiar with how the WB reacts and behaves. This will allow you to compare the two in the datalog and figure out if they are tracking together or if there are key engine conditions that consistently have the two sensors contradict each other. From the few tunes I've seen from others, it seems the HEGOs register AFRs differently than the WBs do and thus sometimes report conditions differently than the WB in the same pipe. In the logs I remember looking at, the HEGO would be reporting conditions deep in the .7v range (rich), but the WB would be reporting 15s. Then at other times, they would track perfectly. You might also use the WB's software to increase the responsiveness of your WB feedback signal to make sure the WB controller isn't over-smoothing the values. instruction: Explain boost control in ECU tuning
response: when cold, the cylinder warms up VERY fast. Fuel on the walls is in direct contact with flame so any fuel there disappears pretty quickly. And with sufficient vacuum, the fuel is more volatile and evaporates much more easily. Even water evaporates more easily in a vacuum. If you've never seen this demonstrated, you can get clear vacuum jars that you can connect a vacuum pump to and literally watch water BOIL at room temp if your pump is capable of pulling a deep vacuum. Gasoline and even ethanol are more volatile than water is so they will evaporate much more easily with far less vacuum thus eliminating this as a concern most of the time. Now once the engine is warm, you have both vacuum AND heat to coerce the fuel into a gas. So even if you have injectors firing on closed intake valves, you are likely to just evaporate the liquid fuel right into the port before it is even aspirated. Now this is at idle and moderate loads. Under WOT, you are back at near atmospheric pressure or ABOVE atmospheric pressure in the case of boosted applications, so you don't have vacuum helping with atomization. However what you are describing sounds more like the problem is AFR. It takes the EEC about a minute to get into Closed Loop on a warm start with stock values. You can do a few different things to combat this. Reduce the time it takes to enter Closed Loop using the scalar OPCLT3. I personally have Closed Loop being entered after 32 seconds for cold, warm, or hot conditions. My engine seems to work well with this. Although if you do reduce this, I found I also needed to reduce the scaling function FN018B to not exceed 30 seconds. For some unknown reason, when this function extended "startup" beyond any of the OPCLTx scalars, the EEC never entered Closed Loop and just stayed in OL. That makes no sense to me, but I never investigated it. After updating the scaling function, CL worked normally, entering after 32 seconds of startup time, and all was well. Lean out your Open Loop AFRs in the Base OL Fuel Table (FN1307) for the ECT/Loads your engine idles at so the startup won't be quite so rich. Once you decide for sure which injectors you are going with, you can look up what all those details are. If you can't find that info, close-enough is good enough for starters. As for telling the computer how much boost you want to run, that's a different story. It's a bit more complicated, but once you understand the basics of how the EEC does fuel and spark management, you'll see it isn't rocket science. It's just a lot of details to keep straight and organize. But once you get to tuning a running vehicle, learning all that stuff should be a lot more fun than just talking about it. You'll get FAR more knowledge once you see the numbers before your eyes than you can prior. But some things are good to ask about now. For instance, here's a list of things you need to start familiarizing yourself with: LAMBSE (commanded AFR, not actual AFR) KAMRF (learned fuel trim) Injector PW and how Duty Cycle is calculated based on PW Load vs Load% (advanced topic with 2 schools of thought that both have merit...

Using COBBs Accessport manager, the unit itself can be plugged in and updated. Also, Check your DAM reading too. If the default (on the OTS map) is set to 0.50 (varies between maps / years) and isnt 1.00 , the full amount of possible power isn't being applied (by way of timing advance) , which would certainly lead to sluggish and reduced feelings of power and response. response: on throttle position or while deccelerating. Makes sense since thats what needs to happen to adjust fuel, however while doing a cruise around town, i noticed that the car started bucking again while changing gears... That might be solveable by increasing the accel-enrichment or transient enrichment some. However what you also want to check is what the LAMBSEs are before the shift and what they are trying to get to after the shift. If those numbers are drastically different, then that's where the real problem is. Ideally you want the required LAMBSE values the same at all Closed Loop conditions (cruising, light decel, shifting, moderate acceleration). However until you get your MAF curve and Injector Slope/BP stuff dialed in, that's not going to happen. LAMBSEs will be all over the place. So if you have LAMBSEs in the 1.05s while cruising, then when you shift the engine needs the LAMBSEs in the .9s, you'll run lean until the EEC can get the LAMBSEs worked down. During that lean-burn time, the HEGOs will read .0024 (lean) and the engine's going to run like crap with stumbling, hesitation, and surging. The common problem when shifting is that decels or drops in load are usually rich....

What is happening, even though the MAFV's are the same at different rpm's, the result is that the injector pulsewidth HAVE to be different. Think about it, same MAF means same amount of air. If you have the same amount of air, what else do you need? Same amount of fuel. So if the engine is spinning faster and injectors are firing more often, then... the need to squirt less fuel each time. If it's turning slower, they fire less often so then need to squirt longer to get the same amount of fuel. So, if you get the right squirt at one rpm (one pulsewidth) but the wrong amount at a different pulsewidth, then you're injector settings are still wrong. Ray Top cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: Please explain how load is figured Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Apr 02, 2013 7:35 am In short, Load is a percentage of airflow going into the engine relative to the engine's theoretical max airflow displacement. So if an engine has a displacement of 302 cubic inches, then IF the engine were flowing 302 cubic inches of air for every 2 revolutions of the crank, the Load should calculate out to 100%. Note Cubic Inch or Liters are measures of volume, not mass. However the actual calculation is not that simple since what the computer needs is a mass value. The device the computer uses to detect airflow is either a Manifold Absolute Pressure (MAP) sensor, Vane Airflow Sensor (VAF), or a Mass Air Flow (MAF) sensor. Neither of these measure air in terms of volume, which is what CID is. The MAP sensor is used in Speed-Density setups. This is where the manifold's pressure, along with RPM, Air Temp, knowledge of the engine's CID, and a look-up table are used to calculate...

response: 39lb injectors used in DOHC Cobras? If so, then it doesn't mean it is the end of the world using them in a non DOHC engine, but they will wall-wet more than traditional injectors will. Here's a Tech doc on it: Don't use Ford Cobra 39lb Injectors on single valve engines If the video doesn't work anymore, it would've shown a V-shaped spray pattern produced by these injectors. On newer mod motors, the intake ports are wide, not tall. And on DOHCs with 2 intake valves, each stream of the V-pattern directs fuel to each valve. However on an older engine, the ports are tall and skinny. So a V-pattern just sprays fuel right into the side walls of the head. My guess is you can alleviate some of the negative affects by simply installing them in a traditional engine side-ways or turned. It doesn't eliminate the problem, but it might help.?.?.? Also altering your tune to inject during significant airflow should also help keep fuel from being sprayed against the walls. Stock A9L values have the fuel spray ended before the intake valve has begun to crack open at lower RPM/Loads. In most cases if you are anywhere near sea level, its going to get boost creep, and in many cases dangerous levels of it, to the point of possible catastrophic engine damage. The internal wastegate port becomes overwhelmed with trying to keep up with the EMAP ( exhaust manifold pressure ) occurring in the headers and uppipe, which then in turn forces exhaust gasses to take another path, which in most cases, is back through the turbine, causing it to spool more and increase boost when not asked to (hence: creep) . response: to not cause misfiring. The retarded timing also helps smooth out the erratic cylinder filling (which makes things smoother) and tends to "deaden" the stronger pulses when the cylinder does fill well. I think it also increases the chances of lighting a diluted mixture due to the effective compression being higher (the ignitable molecules are closer together). Another consideration is fuel mixture. If the fuel mixture is not quite where you want it, I think it's better to error on the slightly rich side. This is due to the fact that a lean mixture burns faster (efectively advancing the timing) and it is more likely to not burn completely (ignitable molecules are farther apart). You can data log the load-rpm range where the engine bucks, and retard the timing only in those cells. This way when you roll into the throttle you will still have the advance you need to accelerate. Try to blend the timing on the border cells so that you dont suddenly jump from 15 degrees of less timing to full timing in one cell. Thats it. response: I have a stage 2 2010 XT. Stock except for Accessport and a CNT downpipe with Cat. Running OTS Cobb stage 2 LWG map. When I first changed the pipe, everything looked good. I did a bunch of pulls and showed ZERO timing reductions in Feedback Knock and Fine Knock Learning. After a few weeks, I called it good and stopped really checking. Then summer came. Fiddling around with the AP returning from a long trip and just scrolling through the instant monitoring selections, I noticed some surprisingly high fine knock learning values, high defined as pulling 3-4* of timing out. I then ***'d when I moved to DAM and found it at .8- unhappy. At the time, I figured I picked up a crap tank of gas, but I've been monitoring it much closer since then. What I am finding is still NO knock events at full, mid, or even anything beyond a hair's breadth on the throttle, but tons just off idle- about 20% throttle. Boost at 1-3 PSI. When it boosts beyond that, open throttle a bit, it goes away. But there, very high timing reductions. This is sustained knock while cruising, not see when moving through that RPM range... How high? response: to bring it in to a shop to get the downpipe modified. The PTE had a bigger compressor housing. The housing touches the valve cover and forces the turbo to be angled at a different place than the smaller 55mm On3 turbo. The turbo also comes in contact with the hood and rubs nonstop. Not much i can do about that. But be sure to buy the right oil fittings to clear the hood as well. Had to buy an 90 degree 1/8 NPT female to male fitting to compliment the 0.035 oil restrictor i had. This is also why you want to force open loop and kill adaptives. If you are driving the car in closed loop you are probably fouling the oil. The extra air in the exhaust is making the computer see lean and it is going to increase fuel to compensate. The actual AFR in the cylinder is higher than what the computer is interpreting. response: TX Re: Tuning MAF to blowthrough Quote Post by nhudtwalcker » Sun Mar 06, 2022 12:45 pm cgrey8 wrote: ↑ Sun Mar 06, 2022 10:47 am As far as I know, most stock MAFs are not blow-thru tolerant. IIRC, they read WAY HIGHER than actual flow values. I recall someone many years back trying to blow-thru an LMAF and never could get it right. They abandoned the LMAF and went to a PMAS HPX, I think, and had no trouble at all. Regardless what aftermarket MAF you do decide on, just make sure it is a blow-thru capable MAF. Not all aftermarket MAFs are blow-thru tolerant. Also if you install a blow-off valve, make sure it blows off BEFORE the MAF otherwise the MAF will be measuring and reporting air to the EEC that is being vented to atmosphere and not meeting with the fuel the EEC will be matching to it resulting in overly rich conditions during blow-off. This is a common mistake for people running superchargers. However because you are running a turbo, you have the option to bleed on the exhaust side, not the intake side to avoid this. instruction: Explain boost control in ECU tuning
response: = pre-position airflow measured in lbs/min The calculated pre-position airflow increment is added to an adaptively-corrected idle flow requirement (DESMAF) prior to output of the ISC duty cycle. Pre-position airflow (DASPOT) is a function of the difference between a filtered throttle position (DSTPBR) and a throttle position equal to the closed throttle breakpoint (RATCH + DELHYS). This value is clipped to zero, as a minimum, if the difference becomes a negative value. DELHYS should be set equal to DELTA + HYSTS (the closed throttle breakpoint). DASPOT can be clipped to DASMIN as a minimum if vehicle speed is high enough to prepare for declutch. During closed throttle mode, the DASPOT airflow is "bled off" by decrementing it. This action smoothes the transition into RPM control by gradually eliminating the DASPOT contribution to the idle airflow, DESMAF. The bleed rate is determined by FN879, unless clipped to DASMIN. When vehicle speed falls below DASMPH, normal bleed off will resume. DESMAF = FN875N/D * FN1861 DASMIN = Minimum DASPOT clip for declutch, lbs/min (i.e. keep at this amount of airflow, then resume normal bleed off when vehicle speed falls below DASMPH) DASMPH = Minimu...

response: I have a 2010 Honda Odyssey and live in a country with very poor quality unleaded gasoline. All the gas stations sell Octane booster to put in each time you fill up. Is it wise to use this stuff? Yes, octane booster can help if your engine is pinging or acting sluggish due to the knock sensor retarding timing. Just be sure the booster doesn’t contain any lead compound. Thanks. A friend here said that it is not worth the plastic bottle they sell it in. What’s bad about the gas, if you know? If it’s contaminated or low on detergents and other typical additives, then octane booster won’t really help, but a good fuel additive like Techron might. If you need higher octane, then it does work. But I don’t think an Odyssey has a high compression engine, so it is probably OK to go without. Instead, change your fuel filter more often. I am certainly not an expert, but have been told that a study was done on the gas and it rated at 65 octane. I have a Mazda 5 ('07) and the new Honda. Both are American specs, so were not designed to run on such low octane. I can’t say I have noticed a difference in performance when filling with or without the octane booster.

response: The issue isn't the limitations. The ECU predicts certain response times for events to occur. Exceed these, and check engine lights and other pita things can occur. That's why lots of people experience CEL's with lightweight flywheels. The ECU thinks misfiring is occurring because the engine isn't adhering to "normal" response time parameters. So, go easy on it and it'll behave fine and you'll get home with no reason to head back to the dealership to pull and erase codes. 09 SWP Outback 2.5XT 5MT 263whp, 337 lb-ft 98 Forester S Save Share Like The issue isn't the limitations. response: Im trying to get my truck to run again (1997 Dodge Ram 1500 5.2l) but one problem, Fuel Pump wont turn on. My Volt Meter is saying that i have power going to it but its not turning on. Fuel pump & Relay is fine. Just no power to the Fuel Pump to turn it on. We’ve tested just about everything and we still dont know what’s causing it to do this You contradicted yourself… first you say you HAVE power to the pump, then you say there is NO power to the pump… Which is it? If there is power at the pump AND a good ground and the pump doesn’t run, the pump is bad. If there is power at the relay and no power at the pump AND a good ground at the pump, there is a broken wire between the relay and pump. Yeah i kinda did there. But i fixed the problem by just moving 2 Relays from R5 & R6 to R8 & R9 and the Fuel Pump turned on. R5 & R6 is Fog Lamp/Dual Tank 1 & 2, which isnt needed for the Truck to run. But R8 & R9 is Trailer & Horn. Idk why the Fuel Pump is Connected to either R8 or R9. But My Problem is now Solved.

response: I'm at 47k and wondering if this is something I should start considering. I haven't seen anyone post that they had it done on their N55. If anyone has before and after pics, please post them. I'm curious how much build up there is on these. I know it's less than N54's but don't know how much. Thanks! I have cleaned quite a few N55's. I normally recommend them to be cleaned at around your mileage where I have received positive reviews after the clean. The shape of the carbon is not so bad to the eye and it looks like there is much less carbon. The issue is if you look at it with the valves open a crust forms around the valve seat which creates a type of negative venturi that I would imagine bounces the flow straight into the valve. The first one I opened I thought I shouldn't even bother and did it anyway. The client called me when he got home and was ecstatic. I guess if I owned a N55 I would look at doing it around 60,000miles or so but its all relative to the smoothness of the motor and if you realize things are go a miss.

response: cgrey8 Website Re: Car runs rich down hills? Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon May 12, 2014 12:47 pm If DFSO isn't kicking in soon enough, I'm sure there's a scalar somewhere that will activate DFSO much quicker than 10 seconds. I think mine kicks in within 1 second of being at applicable decel conditions. I don't remember if that's something I had to adjust to make happen or if that was there by default in the X3Z.bin that my tune is based on. As for correcting the rich condition even without DFSO, there's a few different possibilities. A likely cause is the Injector Offset function adding too much fuel when it doesn't need to. You could reduce the entire Offset function and see what that does for you. But this may force you to re-evaluate your Injector Slope/BP values since reducing offset will likely cause you to reduce your low-slope. Not a guarantee, but a possibility. Another option is to reduce the MAF values at the voltages you are running super-lean at. If idle exists at these same voltages, this may have an affect on idle, but it may not. And yet another option is to go to the MAF Backflow table and pull fuel while at RPM/Loads that represent decel conditions. Multiple ways to s...

response: I just bought a new bucket for $285. I have the FFTEC/Vishnu inline pump also and it has the connections that are plug and play, but you still need to tap the power. Best way to do that is to pull the stock connection from the bottom of the bucket lid and slide the female leads out of the light brown connector. Then wrap your power leads around the base of the stock power wires and solder your power leads for your inline. Slide the female leads back into the light brown connector and plug it back into the bottom of the bucket lid. If you have to remove it, you can and it would be hard to see where you attached the power. Based on that description...If installed correctly...the 255 inline would/will be no more difficult to swap out than the Vishnu. You can get the same female bundy fitting to make the stock LPFP connection and order the male bundy fitting for your 255 pump to make the stock connection to the orange fuel line. Then it's just electrical. I think somebody did a DIY for it. Yes I think ultimately they are going to be about roughly the same install if I have to tap into the power with both applications. instruction: Explain fuel mapping in ECU tuning
response: economy, mainly make sure the scaler is very close (the 3D one helps) and the jb4 all map afr is zero'd out for posterity (not sure if it's active with the flash). I also try to get load similar to my main boost curves. Anything with E85 is going to take a substantial hit in fuel economy. With a static value in the scaler and load targets far away from the actual boost I'd frequently see negative trims. Nothing wrong with that and the jb4 does well keeping things in check, but negative trims mean you've been wasting fuel. I like to keep them slightly positive, and the 3D scaler helps a lot especially for the cruise and idle areas, on my car at least. I like to primarily use the jb4 for boost and features, not trim overhead. But seriously ethanol takes much more fuel, especially if you're on the gas. If that's what people are complaining about there's really no fix. Any idea what you and Ken modified? I've tried several different settings to improve fuel economy but nothing really helped. response: the same application IF the 24lb injector can satisfy the demand. However in practice, injectors don't operate just at WOT. They operate at WOT, high load, moderate load, cruising, idle, etc. In the cruise and idle conditions, we are looking for more than just performance. We need fuel economy, smoothness, and in some cases, emissions compliance...most of which are easier attained with smaller injectors than larger ones. So the optimal injector size is big enough to get the job done at WOT, but no bigger. So if your 24lb injectors are not maxing out or getting into the 90% duty cycle range, then you should stick with them. They will give you better non-WOT performance. However if you are planning substantial mods (i.e. larger cam, better intake, better heads, stroke, forced induction, etc) then you will likely want to increase the injector size if you believe the performance increase will be enough to max-out the 24lbers. If you will just barely be maxing them out, you may be able to continue using 24s with a higher fuel pressure...assuming you have an adjustable FPR. instruction: Explain fuel mapping in ECU tuning
response: have a tuner, buy some larger injectors and a used MAF that's large enough to handle the airflow. They don't even have to match. Just get the injector slopes and your new MAF curve into the tune and start fine tuning it. With a tuner, the MAF doesn't necessarily have to be tuned for specific injectors. The injectors and MAF just need to be big enough to handle the demand. However if you are trying to do this without a tuner, then upgrade the injectors to say some used 24lb injectors from eBay and get a C&L or ProM that's tuned for 24lb injectors to fool the EEC into running the 24s. Instead of replacing your 19s with 24s, another option that "might" work is to put an adjustable FPR on the fuel rails and boost the pressure up to about 44lbs which should make your 19s act more like 24s. This along with the MAF tuned for 24lb injectors might save you from having to take the top intake and rails off your motor. My opinion is if you are running a supercharger, you really need to "tune" the EEC to get the best performance from it and to get a "safer" AFR at WOT. response: What I have is an 89 Ranger that I'm transplanting a 97 Explorer 5.0L V8 motor into. After investigating options of how to keep the Explorer motor's computer and harness, I found it much more practical to retrofit the motor with 89-93 Mustang 5.0L sensors and wiring harness then control it with an A9L or A9P ECM. So far, every engine sensor the Mustang A9P I have is expecting has been fitted, however the 97 Explorer V8s don't have a smog pump and thus the front accessory brackets don't make provisions for one to be added. This doesn't pose a legal emissions problem for me since the original engine is newer than my truck and didn't require a smog pump in 97. However the Mustang A9P computer is still going to throw codes because it expects the two Secondar Air solenoids to be there. I've heard putting resistors on the Secondary Solenoid lines will fool the computer into believing they really are there, but that seems more of a hack than a real fix especially since I'm further assuming the ECM is going to expect the MAF to show airflow changes when those solenoids are bypassing air to the exhaust line (or dumping to atmosphere) during KOER tests. PRLDSW is only supposed to define how PERLOAD (aka Load%) is calculated. Either it is equal to Load or it is equal to Load/PEAK_LOAD. But once that determination has been made, PERLOAD is calculated and seems to follow the same behavior from that point on. So I'm confused by how your tune was returning to Closed Loop when FN320A was Zero'd out to force OL. As for FN035, you are right, that is only being used when PRLDSW is set to Load Scale. But it is not being used instead of FN320A, but rather in addition to. All this ties back into the long debated discussion of Load vs Load%. And the only reason to Load Scale is if you want the EEC to vary OL fueling based on Barometric Pressure. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z...

From there, setup to datalog the HEGOs too and watch the HEGOs during crank and after crank. If they run rich right at crank, and then dip to 0v at the same time the motor begins stumbling, then you'll know you got the same leanout problem others have had right at crank. Otherwise its likely running too rich as you suspected. Even with the WB, you'll need to give it some time to warm up before attempting the crank so you know you are getting fairly accurate readings. Other tidbits to note: If it is too lean, the engine will stumble to a low RPM and run really bad and almost conk out. instruction: When I get gas the dash says "low oil pressure stop engine" - Power/Fuel - Car Talk Community
response: Whether I put $20 in my tank or fill it up, 80% of the time when I turn the car on after putting gas in it the dash says “low oil pressure stop engine” for about 30 seconds. "When I get gas the dash says “low oil pressure stop engine” It amazes me how smart that cars have become. No big deal, it will resolve when you do the next oil change with a new filter. When you fill up the gas tank, even if the engine is turned completely off, the evap system may still be using electrical power operating valves and such to accommodate the fueling. When you restart it takes a couple of seconds to refill the filter causing the low oil pressure warning. When the car gets it’s first oil change after that and “normal” oil is added the problems show up. I am not sure about the getting gas connection, but as I have found out the oil pressure guage in my trailblazer is an estimated value, and the light is related to actual readings.

response: beyond pretty painless and a joyful experience. Cheers! We have quite a few customers in CO and other higher elevation places so hopefully a few can chime in. But what I was trying to tell you via email was that the JB+ is a relatively simple device that exploits the DME, fooling it in thinking the air is less dense than it actually is. Which works well at sea level. It can work well at elevation also but the amount of power vs. stock you can gain using that method drops as a function of elevation. If you are doing a lot of elevation changes, you'd have to turn the dial down towards the minimum setting to avoid false 30FF boost under target codes. Which isn't fun. Still, if you like what you have and just want 20hp more, the JB+ at a lower setting is a simple to install and easy to try option. You get six months to trade it up to a JB4 as well should you decide you want more. The JB4 is a much more complex and robust device. How would you explain why my car, running my prevous set-up(small greddy turbo), likes as much as 50deg cam advance at 8psi and has a vtec x-over of 4200rpm? This is the result of about 120 dyno pulls while testing this set-up. We found the unthinkable. The backpressure from the little turbo was nowhere near what it was on other set-ups that were identical to this one. The engine liked as much overlap as most N/A engines, if not more! This was ubsurd to think, but it was true. It even stumped Doug as well when i told him. Most CN set-ups, which feature much larger turbine sections, didn't want more than 20-30deg of cam advance. This pointed to a very good head and exhaust. You simply cannot calculate factory tolerances into the equation without knowing what you are dealing with first. This requires the use of a dyno. Also, i see no mention of ignition timing, which is the most critical part. You cannot tune ignition timing (other than retarding timing at points of knock) safely without a dyno. instruction: Explain fuel mapping in ECU tuning
response: the injectors themselves. Assuming your fuel rail pressure is in the 43-44 PSI range, the most likely location of the error is the MAF curve. If the MAF curve is indicating more air is coming into the engine than actual, then the datalogs would suggest that you need to pull fuel using the injector slopes. Raising the slope value higher does just that. As long as the Injector Slopes are within a few points of what they are supposed to be, then I wouldn't be terribly concerned about it. Although if you are still running a stock FPR (39PSI), then it is odd that you would actually calculate slopes higher than advertised...but still possible if there is excessive error in the MAF curve. If you are really that worried about it, you can try dividing the entire MAF curve by a given amount and see if that brings your Slopes in closer. But that's a lot of work redialing in, what's basically all new MAF curve and Injector Slope/BP values. Also note that doing this would have the effect of lowering your calculated Load which may cause you to revisit your Spark tables as well. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer...

response: that might be. In the case of E85, Closed Loop will now be targeting 9.76 AFR (or whatever E85's stoic AFR is). Although in this scenario, it's possible the LAMBSE adjustable limit would be hit before stoic is found. I believe decipha's A9L2 has those limits widened for instances where this might occur. The point I'm trying to make is that while in Closed Loop, the Closed Loop algorithm targets to switch the HEGOs independent of what the Z_AFR scalar is set to. The influence the Z_AFR scalar has is the LAMBSE values Closed Loop finds will be different if a change to Z_AFR is made. For example if a user loads up a Quarterhorse with 2 tunes, then flips between them while in Closed Loop with the only difference being a change to Z_AFR scalar. Regardless which tune is active, Closed Loop will settle into ~1.00 lambda for the fuel being burned although the LAMBSE values Closed Loop hones in on will be slightly different. Since the tune setup for E10 will be calculating slightly more fuel than the gasoline tune, Closed Loop will see a rich condition when a transition from the gasoline to E10 tune is made and will adjust LAMBSEs to pull that same amount back out to attain 1.00 lambda. instruction: Explain ignition timing in ECU tuning
response: is the 1st time that the car has behaved this good cold. It usually stalls and I have to restart it. Took it for a drive and the hesitation was still there :( Up to now, everything that I have read regarding bringing the load down has been around lowering the engine displacement. It was not until I read a post by BobCat and JuiceSC that I figured that I would change the engine displacement by increasing it by the same amount as the MAF functions. My engine size is 317, so I multiplied it by 42/19 (2.21) and got 700.73 That high of a number made me a little bit nervous, so I fattened up the A/F and lowered the timing quite a bit in the 2000-4000 range (load 30% on up). There have always been factors from one tank to the next that my gas mileage would fluctuate ±4mpg. What could cause this sudden drop in mpg? They should be around 4k ohms each in order to get the correct duration of spark. Also consider that the actual difference in number of gallons dispensed per fill up is probably something like 1-2 gallons and when you’re dealing with such a small difference a lot of generally minor factors can make a noticeable difference. For example, a few extra cold starts or prolonged idling (both of which are likely to occur in a shop) will easily burn a gallon or so of gas and the minor variations in accuracy and cut-off point with gas pumps can also amount to maybe a quart or two, which along with normal variation in driving conditions could easily explain the discrepancy.

MikeDrives1 4,329 posts · Joined 2010 Add to quote #9 · Feb 17, 2021 The factory subaru tuning strategy for NA 4-cyls is quite aggressive and to the max, so there is almost NO power to be gained by calibration means. Even on 3.6R's ive tuned, you only get a marginal amount more. the BEST thing you can do for easy HP.... run 91 or better octane fuel in there. These NA guys knock and knock a LOT. They have the same knock strategy layout as all the turbo models with knock learning and DAM systems, and in almost all cases of NA's ive worked on that run regular, the DAM is below 0.50 with tons of learned knock. The best and easiest pick-me-up for these cars is to keep on top of maintenance and run 91 or better... Makes the ECU happy and it will run more timing advance (happily and relatively knock free) which equates to a little more power, by factory design. Its not an overnight thing though, its going to take a tank or two of gas for the ECU

instruction: Explain dyno tuning in ECU tuning
response: The car drove oK but had a wondering idle and smelled a bit rich. It would occasionally die when shifted from drive to neutral or park as the idle would quickly jump up and then subsequently drop and die. It would often times have to be restarted when shifting from drive to reverse when parking or maneuvering in the driveway. First Adjustment The first adjustment I made was to pull the spout connector and IAB connector and adjust the throttle stop until the engine could idle. This put the TPS sensor over 1.0 volts so I drilled the mounting holes larger on the tps so I could adjust it back below 1.0 volt. I ended up with it set at .95 volts. I plugged the spout and IAB connector back in and after a bit of adjusting, the idle improved but still wondered. It was a little less likely to stumble and die when shifted between park/neutral and drive than previously but still was unstable. Second Adjustment Speculating that the camshaft was causing the engine to run at less volumetric efficiency below 2500 rpm than the factory cam, I took a wild guess and reduced the VE table by 10% below 2500 rpm. For safety, I did not change the highest load cells (top row) or the lowest load cells

response: the Fuel Startup Table (FN1306) must be scaled not to exceed the OPCLT times. I can't explain this in code, but while experimenting, I found that if FN1306 was scaled to be active higher than OPCLT to say 45 seconds, then CL would somehow be suppressed and you'd stay in OL even beyond 45 seconds. I didn't go CL for well over 5 minutes. I can't say this is readily reproducible. I had this problem long ago when I was messing with these parameters. When I realized the "overlap", I rescaled the FN1306 table to be at the top row by 30 seconds with OPCLT1, 2, and 3 set to 32 seconds. Once I did that, all worked as expected and has worked as expected since. I can't say I pay attention to when I go CL every time I go CL, but I do pay attention to it most of the time and I think I would notice if it didn't go CL shortly after crank especially on cold days. The biggest one being CalCon datalogs Injector PW wrong. It's close, but wrong and thus trying to tune Injector Slopes using CalCon datalogs will prove most frustrating because no matter how much you adjust, your slopes will always recalculate to something smaller due to the inaccuracy. We lived with that for YEARS before we figured out Calcon was just doing flat out wrong. And since you can't change the behavior of Calcon, people that use it are just stuck with it. But in BE, we had the ability to correct the problem and now slope calcs from EA come out far more accurate than they did with CalCon. Another thing, CalEdit mislabelled some of the spark tables. This will let you dial in the MAF curve by logging, using EA to compute a new curve, drive and log some more and repeat the process a few times varying the drive conditions as much as possible. Don't forget to clear the KAMRF's with each subsequent curve you load. Keep it out of Open Loop as much as possible and when you use EA to compute the cruve select the option that only looks at Closed Loop operation. Once you have the low and mid-range of the curve dialed in pretty well you can fine tune the slopes, injector break point and so on. The top end of the curve requires a wide band O2 sensor. If you are willing to lay down some cash you might find a dyno operator willing to work with you to get the top end of the curve dialed in. The guy I go to does a pull, gives me the AFR vs RPM data that I compare with my BE log for the run and I adjust the MAF curve accordingly. Third thing is gear readout. Since the car has to stay coded as a manual and use the "manual" way of calculating gear (basically a formula using road speed, rpm, final ratio, etc), the DME and JB4 have no clue what gear the car is actually in (since all the slip in the torque converter can have the car at the same speed and the same rpm in virtually every gear). This creates issues for things like boost by gear. I've worked out the serial protocol for the EZ TCU and can read the gear parameter so I may end up making a little chip to feed that into the JB4. As far as the throttle closures, I really need to get my rpm limiter out of the way and just shift it a tad earlier to see if that will clean it up. response: are closer than you were at least for that day. Borderline ping is the max advance the engine can handle before detonation occurs. You can tune this one yourself...just use your ears. And again, fuel, air temp, engine mood, moon&stars, etc also affect this one too. But at least you can tweak if next week's new moon position makes your car ping more than last week. (BTW, I'm kidding about the moon-n-stars affects...I hope that much was obvious) Moving forward, for any given RPM/Load, these don't always exist at the same place. Thus at some RPM/Loads, it's possible to exceed your advance for Max torque, but not be pinging yet. Likewise at other RPM/Loads, you may ping, but if you advanced a little further anyway, you might could get a little more torque out of'er while upsetting small children with the pinging noise and loud mufflers. In an ideal situation, you don't want to exceed either of these. Since they don't occur at the same degrees of advance, but are in the same general vicinity, most do-it-yourselfer tuners tune to Ping since that's something that doesn't require a dyno. response: in such a way that it brings the blue line closer to the orange, but in a way that keeps the blue line as smooth as possible. Often the calculated line isn't very smooth. Until you get a finely tuned curve, you want to maintain a curve that's as smooth as possible. This is why I say manually modify the values in the "blue" curve. Also don't bring the blue curve all the way to the orange curve. If there is a BIG difference between them, modify the blue curve by 1/2 the distance between the blue and orange curve. Once you have a modified blue curve that is relatively smooth, save it and transfer that curve over to your tune. Download the modification to your EEC and clear the KAMRFs by either pulling the battery cable or downloading an invalid BIN if you have a selectable tuner like TwEECer (neat trick). Run this MAF curve for a few days. DO NOT go run the MAF curve for 10-15 minutes, then take that log and calculate a new curve. You'll chase your tail doing that. instruction: Explain fuel mapping in ECU tuning
response: they usually do fail to lean (toward 0v) so the EEC is compensating to rich. Since O2 sensor failure is generally a gradual thing the process of the EEC running the motor richer and richer is not usually recognized by the owner until key things start happening like noted loss in fuel economy and bad or hunting idle due to excessive rich AFRs. New O2s will switch briskly across their switch-point and with a high voltage potential at mildly rich conditions. Old, worn-out O2s will switch much more sluggishly and not produce as high of a voltage on the rich swings. And the voltages they do report will correspond to richer mixtures as compared to newer O2s. So during this "wear-down", the EEC will be responding with a mixture that's a tad on the rich side (better a little too rich than a little too lean). Eventually, the O2 will not be able to produce a voltage above the switch-point the EEC is looking for without getting the motor excessively rich. This is when the motor starts getting noticeably worse gas mileage as well as an unstable idle and in some cases, the motor just dies shortly after a deceleration (most typical with automatics). Ultimately, the switch-point won't be attainab...

response: the EEC is receiving. So what exactly is it you are wanting to stabilize? If its spark, that's quite possible. Just find everywhere that you get spark added to/removed, and null that out so there's only 1 place that spark is controlled. Depending on how well your strategy is broken out in your def might change these a bit. It's also worth mention that things like pulling spark due to high ECT or high ACT are there for a reason. I would encourage you to incorporate those into your tuning, not eliminate them. But those are potential sources of inconsistency in spark advance which could result in inconsistencies in performance on the track. Unfortunately fuel delivery isn't nearly as straight forward to stabilize. Fuel is directly related to the MAF readings. There are a number of other controls such as the fuel table and fuel adders, but unstable/inconsistent MAF readings will result in unstable/inconsistent fuel delivery. Ideally, you need to identify what it is, exactly, that is causing the inconsistency by comparing datalogs. Find trends of what produced good output and what didn't. One thing to understand is when you increase the FP in the rails, you change the delay in how long it takes the injectors to open. More pressure pushing down on the plungers mean that it requires more time for the coil to open the plunger against the FP. Then when you get up to 50-60psi, you run into issues with the fuel pump having to keep up, this is amplified if you have larger than stock fuel lines. I had always thought you should lean out the a/f to overcome the water/methanol richening the a/f but it worked better to not do that. I ended up commanding 11.7 a/f and leaving it at that. response: The E60 M5 is supposedly good for 12.3 secs. The F10 M5 is 12.0 secs. So let's keep expectations along those lines. Those are official numbers from BMW. If I can get a 535 E60 to get into that group somewhere, then I say mission accomplished. Nothing to be ashamed of. I think so far LQQKOUT has the world record for a 535 with N54. But obviously any FBO w RB car will bust that by some margin. High 11s might be possible with track tires and high octane fueling. I wouldn't bet against that. Thats true. I also see some guys who are not even FBOs and JB4s in the low to mid 12s. Honestly it really depends on a ton of conditions but I'm willing to bet that RBs+ FBO can at least break 11s if not go deep into the 11s. +1 there are a couple rb 335s knocking on the door of 10s. I would imagine with rbs using meth, e85, or other high octane you could definitely be in the 11s (conditions permitting) And I'm guessing with the e60 M5 weighing 4090 lbs and the F10 M5 weighing 4288 lbs we *should* have some level of advantage? The Xdrive's/Xi's have a great launch advantage. I have seen 60's of even 1.7-1.8 which is blazing quick.

response: 30, 2004 7:45 am Location: Largo, Fl Re: Few loose ?'s Quote Post by DrDirt » Wed Aug 06, 2008 9:13 am What do you have your OL Base Fuel set at for WOT? The stock x3z.bin has 11.9 as the commanded fuel. Did you change it to something else? I've never run anything stock so I may be wrong but those AFR numbers don't look rich to me. But, once you get the turbo on, you definitely don't want to see those AFR and spark numbers at WOT. Depending on how much boost you are running you will want from 11.1 to 11.5 AFR and around 19 spark. Set the desired AFR in the OL base fuel table and make the adjustments to your MAF transfer to bring the AFR into line with what you want. Approach things slowly and carefully with WOT. You want to start out rich and then work you way leaner. Listen carefully for detonation and get out of it immediately if you hear it. But, be aware that you can't always hear detonation so start out with your spark low too and slowly work you way up. You will also have to rescale your sea level loadscaling. response: for MegaSquirt is much lower since it is mean to be a DIY tuner and thus doesn't have all the "baggage" and complication that DIY tuners using the original Ford code often force on you. The biggest limitation of most piggyback tuners are based on the host EEC. The 89-93 Mustang EECs and similar 15MHz EECs have an RPM limitation of somewhere around 6500-6800 with V8s...higher with V6s since there are 2 less cylinders/rev. There's a way to overcome this limitation by overclocking the processor by replacing the 15MHz crystal with an 18MHz chip. This has been done, but with unknown success or unknown side-effects. Newer Ford EECs that are 18MHz from the factory obviously are more immune to this. However if you only need low 6000s from the EEC, then all is well. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top bender460 Tuning Addict Posts: 393 Joined: Thu Sep 07, 2006 12:29 am Re: Multiple tuning solutions, discussion. response: lot of oil. I would set the idle up about 1200 rpm to start with. Talk to the builder on where he wants it to idle, once you get it tuned. Start high until you get it stable. If at all possible get the MAF transfer curve for your MAF meter. If at all possible get the specs for your injectors. If you have neither of these it would be very hard for a beginner. You need something to start with that is very close to reality. Get your displacement set and get the MAF very close before loading the engine Leave the factory timing alone until you get the fuel right. Get a wide band O2. Force it to open loop and set the entire fuel table to lamda 1.0 to start with. Do not go more than half throttle that lean. Get the fuel to equal the commanded lamda. Do not load the engine if the fuel is lean. This should all be right before you ever put it into gear. Once you get the part throttle right, then move on to a rich lambda for high loads. response: didn't notice, but it also could be a flat-tappet cam too which would explain the lower numbers. The good news is that it should be well behaved at idle...even if it doesn't scream at the high RPMs. Commenting on the injector timing, red values in the timing is perfectly normal. All that's doing is telling you that at that RPM/Load, the start time will need to be backed up OR the injector will continue firing after the intake valve has closed which isn't a good thing. To solve that problem, manually cap the values in your tune to around 550 and you'll avoid any problems with the injector firing too late at high RPM/Loads. Injector timing is most meaningful at the lower and cruising RPM/Loads anyway and you should be able to meet your injector timing desires for those conditions no problem. As for the 24s in a 351, I've heard that over and over with no technical confirmation other than people saying "it's a bigger engine." The CID has nothing to do with the injector size. There are 351s that barely make 200hp. There are 289s that can produce well over 400hp. What affects injector size is how much air the engine can aspirate. response: header pipe, not the lack of fuel. I think it would be more likely that those two injectors are open all the time and at idle they are basically flodding those two cylinders. Very possibly your injector harness could be flawed and is going to ground on just those two injectors holding them open. Remember when the EEC turns the injector ON, it is actually completing the circuit by taking the injector wire to ground. I would check the two wires going into each of the two injectors. While running one of the wires should always be at 12 volts. The second wire should be cycling from 12 volts to zero volts. You could check this at idle. An oscilloscope would be the easiest way to check this but if you don't have one, take a 12 volt light bulb, solder two wires to it to use as probes and test with one lead at ground and the second lead as your test probe. Good luck with it! instruction: Explain fuel mapping in ECU tuning
response: not designed to accept a Wideband as an analog input feedback mechanism for the purpose of fuel control. The Ford EEC is only looking for a feedback of rich or lean. It has no way to do something different when things are slightly richer than commanded value vs way off of commanded value. So the short answer is no. You can't get "Full Time Closed Loop" control with stock EEC-IV/V coding. However the stock tunes are setup to apply info learned while at Closed Loop conditions at WOT conditions hence why the Adaptive Control table has negative values up on the WOT Load rows. Ford presumably determined that if the EEC was off at those cruising loads, it would be about as off at WOT conditions. How they determined that, I have no clue. It's certainly not safe for us DIY tuners to make those same assumptions. A tune can be perfectly dialed in at cruising RPM/Loads and way off at WOT. So always recommend people removing that stock behavior from the Adaptive Control table. But that's just me... response: Hey guys. I have a 08 335i coupe. Weeks ago, the cluster told me I have a bulb out somewhere so several times, I pulled the car into a dark garage and hunted for the mysterious dead bulb. I've ruled out headlight, brake light(even the third upper one), turn signals, hazards, reverse, side markers, angel eyes, fog, pretty much all the external bulbs. I had coding done to leave the front LED amber lights in the headlights off so the angel eyes looked better so they're off but never through a bulb-out code. Does the cluster notice also pertain to interior lights? The code comes on just after startup; day or night. Has anyone else run into this? For the life of me, I can't find a dead bulb. I believe bulb current is monitored and can report a "bad" bulb even before the actual bulb burns out. I had been chasing "Break Light" bulbs that were reported bad just like you without much luck. Look for a bulb that no longer looks clear but may have a silverly looking coating on the inside of the bulb.... vaporized bulb filament. That one is most likely you problem. Also a code reader can tell you the exact bulb to replace if you do not have IDrive.

response: Western Australia. Re: Variable reluctance v's hall effect speed sensors Quote Post by xd41efisc » Tue Nov 22, 2011 7:33 am Yes it can be done, I have done to A9L, L0E1 and C0S. L0E1 and C0S are Supercharged V6 Thunderbird ECUs, the use the same basic hardware layout as A9L. What I did was looked at a Series 1 EB Falcon ECU (same layout as A9L), and traced out what was different in the circuitry for pin 3 and 6. Off memory you don't need to use pin 3, you only use pin 6. The mods involve removing a few diodes, resistors, capacitors, and fitting a link on the back of the board. I am using an XD-XE sender, that has the same type of output as the latter XF-EL sender, the only difference is the amount of pulses / revolution, The XD-XE is 8/rev, the XF-EL is 10. When I have a bit of time I will take some photos of a non moded A9L and a moded A9L, and highlight the mods needed. instruction: IC - Bar/Plate or Tube/Fin? - JB4tech.com - International Turbo Tuning Discussion?
response: Do you want enough CFM to satisfy your RPM requirements = yes Do you want as little pressure drop as available = yes Can you augment intake cooling with additional methods = yes When upping the boost, you are not increasing CFM, you are increasing pressure at the same CFM. This is good, because for the same amount of intake PSI, the turbos do not have to work as hard. What fuel are you using? E85 or meth you should focus primarily on pressure drop. Pressure drop and IAT are the important aspects. A larger core gives more time for the air in the intercooler, aiding in cooler IAT's. The purpose of an intercooler, is to drop IAT, so to answer your question the most directly, cooler IAT's are the most important factor when all else is equal. An intercooler that flows more cfm would suggest for the same CFM, there would be less pressure drop. Less waste = less heat generated. Pump gas in a hot climate you're going to want the best iat suppression you can find.

response: all the way to 0v. Even before I started playing around with the HEGO stuff in my tune, that was normal behavior for them. But I've seen quite a few logs from others where their HEGOs rarely reach 0v under normal Closed Loop operation. I wish I understood what exactly the difference between our setups is to know what that means. But as long as you have a WB and you get the right transfer for it, that shouldn't be a big deal. The important thing is that the EEC is modulating the LAMBSEs up and down to keep the HEGOs switching above and below .423v while at Closed Loop...and yours are. While your EEC is switching the HEGOs, the switching is happening fairly sluggishly at least the way it appears in the log. But looking at a log and witnessing what's happening live are two different things. At some point, you may find there's some fuel economy you can pick up by playing around with things like the HEGO switch-point voltage (only available on GUFx), HEGO Bias, HEGO Amplitude, HEGO Delay, and possibly even in the HEGO functions.
