Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Mar 11, 2009 12:59 pm The idle AFR depends a lot on your cam. The E303 and F303 are both just barely not overlap cams @.050" lobe lift but they are "big" enough that I wouldn't be surprised if you have unburned intake air being scavenged into the exhaust...particularly if you have long-tube headers which enhance scavenging. But I've heard the E303 can allow scavenging of intake air into the exhaust with aftermarket heads that flow well. The F303 has a good 6 degrees of advance compared to the E303 so I would expect it to not scavenge quite as much but that doesn't mean it doesn't. In the cases where you have scavenging of intake air into the exhaust, the HEGOs and WB get confused and think things are leaner than the engine is actually burning. To combat this, most people find they have to force OL and command lean AFRs during idle to get the engine to run right. BTW, no MAF curve I know of is linear, hence why it is a curve. The curve is not by accident. There is some science behind why it is a curve, and not linear like Wideband O2 transfers are. Next topic... Compensation done by Closed Loop and Adaptive Learning are for all fueling conditions, not just the MAF's affect on fueling. The EEC is compensating for error in the MAF curve, error in the injector parameters, possible air leaks into the engine, the engine's combustion behavior itself, and even the fuel you are burning (100% gasoline vs E10 or some other variant). response: One more time, unc@tted *** won't reduce the stress on the turbos, it's the opposite, because the restriction is on the exhaust flow, and the turbo stress is a function of the exhaust flow. More flow = more turbos revs= more stress. running 15 psi with stock *** and unc@tted *** means exactly the same stress for the turbos, as the boost pressure is a function of the exhaust flow applied to the exhaust turbine. Simply not true. Your stuck on defining stress with boost pressure. 15 psi with factory *** is producing more turbine, compressor and combustion heat. This is the whole premise behind limiting boost with stage 1 tunes. If a tuner sets stage 1 boost at 13 psi its because its deemed anything much more produces more heat and stress than they want to releasing to the public long term (or for daily flogging). If 15 psi was 15 psi regardless there would be no DP requirement to up the boost. The additional back pressure is fighting directly against the turbine wheel. This requires more work from the engine to spin the turbine (why *** = quicker spool). Not only does the turbine run hotter but the effects of back pressure go all the way back to the additional work required to push ex...

Cranking strategy is rather blind. It's basically just firing injectors at a given Pulse-width based on the engine temp. But once the engine is running, the EEC wants to transition over to using the MAF. If the MAF is unreliable, there are MAF-failure tables that attempt to guesstimate airflow based on a number of factors, but mainly RPM and TPS. Since this is a table, it thus can be tuned. And if all you care about is idle and WOT, then that is possible...but you are purposely denying yourself the opportunity to get FAR more from that engine. This is why decipha was saying that having the MAF is better, but not required to do what you are trying to do. sbcspeed wrote: ...Being a bottle fed baby, I'd really like to be able to datalog my fuel, timing and knock sensor input if at all possible... response: into the tune along with the MAF's physical installation, there shouldn't be any AFR discrepancies with flow values within the MAF's readable range. You run into problems with on an undersized MAF when the flow exceeds the measurable range of the MAF. When that happens, the MAF cannot communicate a higher flow rate to the EEC so the EEC isn't aware of what the true flowrate is. See the MAF can only send a signal back to the EEC in the 5-5.1v range max. Once the MAF is sending that, if the flow continues to increase, the best it can do is continue to send the same 5v signal. So the EEC doesn't know about the increased air flow and THAT is when you start going lean. Flowrates below this point should be unaffected, again assuming the MAF curve is correct for the hardware you have installed. Does that clarify it a bit? Now from a practical standpoint, you never want to see 5v values. You size the MAF so that the max MAF voltage your engine will create is in the 4.5-4.8v range. response: seems you are under the impression that it is unlikely for one bank to run differently than the other bank. You are looking for ground issues and leaks, but haven't considered that maybe this is just how your engine operates. If you are so confident that both banks are the same, then disable one sensor and run it as a single bank system. This will ensure that both banks get the same amount of fuel. The whole purpose of the stereo o2 sensor system is specifically for this situation. NB o2 sensors are EXTREMELY accurate (more so than a WB, thats for sure), and are not prone to ground plane issues, because even tenths of a volt at the sensor result on only a marginal percentage (2-3) of AFR swing, certainly not 15%. Leaks can certainly cause the symptoms you are seeing, and a ground issue could cause the same to a much lessor degree. dirty fuel injectors, uneven manifold filling characteristics, unequal compression from one bank to the other, etc, etc, all can contribute. Now, you have to wonder if you setup your adaptive mapping to utilize the KAM trim at WOT, would you make more power because of possibly more accurate fueling to both banks.... The catch is the same transfer curve is used for both ACT and ECT. So if you change one, you'd have to change the other as well. Interestingly you may find that GM and Ford sensors are not that different. Ford uses a pretty standard thermistor for both ACT and ECT. Assuming the thermistor is a standard 10k thermistor, I don't know if it is a Precon 10k Type II or Type III, but it wouldn't surprise me if GM is using the same exact physical thermistor. Just looking at the transfer, I can't tell what the thermistor type is since the transfer is volts-to-degrees and most thermistor transfers are published in ohms-to-degrees. This sounds more like a grounding problem. I had a similar problem when I 1st got my 302 into my truck. There was a grounding wire that went from the battery's negative terminal to a ground screw on the body of the truck. That ground wire had fallen off and was causing weird ground loops that would cause the HEGOs to report fine when no electrical loads were ON in the truck. But if I turned my headlight on or turned the dash blower motor on, I could watch my max HEGO voltages go from .6s down to .3s. Once the electrical loads got high enough that the HEGOs couldn't produce above .42v, the engine started trimming richer and richer. response: vacuum canisters supply backup suction to the wastegates to allow the turbo to build boost (it has no connection to the intake manifold). Having a stronger vacuum signal would mean your turbos may build boost faster when pressing the throttle. However those canisters are a vacuum reservoir, I don't believe they actually increase the vacuum as they are just there for situations when the mechanical vacuum pump may not produce enough vacuum for one reason or another such as brake booster hogging the vacuum at low rpms. So if you're experiencing this, then you probably had a leaking vacuum canister or vacuum line from the pump to the wastegates and you'd experience the same thing with no vacuum canisters at all so long as your vacuum pump was healthy and the vacuum leak/issue was addressed. Click to expand... You remember correctly. They are reservoirs. V veer90 Captain Jan 30, 2019 #4 The vacuum canisters were designed with spirited driving in mind, where you're repeatedly smashing the brakes then the gas quickly in succession. With a reservoir more vacuum is available to the wastegates immediately after hard braking. Many people delete them with no issue since they only do highway pu...

instruction: Explain MAF tuning in ECU tuning
response: means is you'll be able to datalog more than just X number of parameters since this device will not only be replacing the EEC's ROM, but also the EEC's RAM. So the Pegasus processor will have DIRECT access to the RAM space any time it needs it to relay what's there to the PC. This differs from the TwEECer in that the TwEECer relies on code hacks to instruct the EEC's processor to relay info from it's memory to the TwEECer so it can be relayed. The Pegasus wouldn't require re-tasking the EEC to do this. That sounds great for the values that we CAN get directly from RAM like Load, Load%, KAMRFs, LAMBSEs RPMs, Spark, InjPW, etc. However this doesn't help for pulling values that must be relayed such as values coming in directly from A/D converters that only the EEC's processor would have access to. In these cases, you'll still be required to hack the EEC's instruction code to have the EEC relay that info to the Pegasus. Fortunately, there's not a lot of these and even the EEC does a fair amount of duplicating of these values. For instance in GUFx defs, the MAFV (IMAF) value is pulled in from the A/D converters, a smoothing/filtering algorithm is applied, then the result is saved in RAM...

response: Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: Injector Slopes. To be or not to be equal? Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Aug 28, 2008 6:32 am Some of it is simplicity. Some of it is "Ford did it on the Cobra, it must be OK to do" mentality. Some of it is it just happens to work well for some people like this. But if you datalog with BE and use EEC Analyzer, then you get the benefit of the Injector Slope Calculator to show you your Injector performance and thus you can find Injector Slope/BP values that fit better. Back when I experimented HEAVILY with this, I found that the Injector Offset curve contributed heavily to what your low slope and breakpoint will be. If you lower that curve, you lower what the low-slope will be. My efforts were to lower it to the point that I could truly make Injector High and Low slopes the same. And I got really close. My slopes went from 17.8H/70L/3BP (yes 70lb for a low slope), to 18.2H/19.8L/6BP which is what I run in my tune today. Once I got the low slope that close to the high slope, things ran a lot more predictable and the need for accuracy on the BP was not nearly as important as it

response: the capacity to maintain 400v once the coil is loading them up. I didn't find any info on what voltage the charge drops to. If I had to guess, I'd say the voltage drops to around 20v (that's a complete guess). Each cap is used to charge the coil in very short succession in order to get multiple spark fires without the typical dwell time normally required to charge the coil. And because the coil is charged using higher-than-12v, it's discharge voltage will be significantly higher. Where a stock coil may be in the 30kv range, an ignition box fired coil can easily be in the 45-60kv range. At low RPMs, the ignition box can recharge the caps in time to re-fire the coil 5, 6, or even 7 times per PIP. However as RPMs rise, there's simply insufficient time for multiple sparks. Once the RPMs are in the 3000 RPM range, there's not enough time to multi-fire the plugs at all, so the box transitions to using all available capacitors in parallel to charge the coil to deliver as solid of a single spark as possible. More capacitors in parallel can deliver more current which makes the charge-voltage on the coil even higher than a single cap can do by itself. This boosts the coil performance in the...

response: 2017 1:59 pm I'm sure there's some AFR that "might" result in this however here are my thoughts... First off this USUALLY only is a concern when the engine is cold and cranking. When the engine is cranking, you can wall-wash due to spraying too much fuel or puddling fuel by spraying on close valves and thus dumping whole droplets into the combustion chamber. Crank is of particular focus of wall wash just because the engine isn't spinning very fast so there's very little air flow to really do a good job of atomizing. Add to this, the vacuum at crank is very low so fuel doesn't "want" to evaporate. Once the engine is running under its own power, even when cold, the cylinder warms up VERY fast. Fuel on the walls is in direct contact with flame so any fuel there disappears pretty quickly. And with sufficient vacuum, the fuel is more volatile and evaporates much more easily. Even water evaporates more easily in a vacuum. If you've never seen this demonstrated, you can get clear vacuum jars that you can connect a vacuum pump to and literally watch water BOIL at room temp if your pump is capable of pulling a deep vacuum. response: at this load point. If you have a MAF voltage of say 1.125 volts , yours will be different at 30% load, you go to that voltage point in the MAF transfer and reduce that kg/hr flow of say70.5 until you get 14.64 (or very close to it) as a wideband reading while datalogging at the flow voltage and rate. You do this for all voltage points on the MAF transfer. This is where EA (or the MAF auto tune in BE) makes life easy. It can be done with Excel and or calculator. You reduce based upon the percentage so 11.58/14.64 = .791 then multiply it with flow 70.5 = 55.76 new flow value at 1.125v. For lean 17/14.64 = 1.1612 multiplied by hypo flow 70.5 new flow 81.86 at 1.125v. Datalog and repeat until your wideband is reading what the ECU is commanding (Lambse). I have been doing this for weeks/months here and there on weekends. ONCE you have your Lambse matching your wideband then your MAF/Injectors are dialed in. NOW if you want to change your fueling you go to the fuel table and put in the AFR you want to acheive, in the relevant load/temp points. instruction: Explain dyno tuning in ECU tuning
response: into each cylinder charge relative to the theoretical MAX for natural aspiration. So for a 5.0L V8, each cylinder is capable of holding 0.625L of air (at atmospheric pressure). Using the MAF feedback along with the RPM, the computer can estimate how much air is actually being aspirated into each cylinder fire. The amount relative to the theoretical max is the Load value. For boosted applications, it's possible to shove MORE than the theoretical max into the engine since the booster is increasing the aspiration pressure well above atmosphere thus making it possible to have Load values above 100%. In the case where you have a 5.0L that the computer thinks is a 5.7L, now you have the computer under-calculating the actual load of the engine. This could be dangerous in that higher spark advances would be commanded than may be safe for the engine given the computer expects engine load to be lower than actual. The only way I know of to compensate for this is to multiply all points on the MAF curve by 1.14 (5.7/5.0). instruction: Explain ignition timing in ECU tuning
response: they fire the injector a little early. When you have a cam and are pushing the injector to fill all available intake valve open time, it can be important to set the injector timing up more precisely. Here's my thinking when I set mine up: My aftermarket cam has some overlap AND I have a supercharger. At low RPM's I don't want the injector firing while the exhaust valve is still open - unburnt gas could pass directly into the exhaust - especially since the KB can make boost just off idle. So I used "trailing edge" and "exhaust valve closed" as my settings at low RPM. Now I know the injector will not fire before the exhaust valve is closed. At higher RPM's, the injector would be on so long using the exhaust closed event that the injector would still be open after the intake valve closed. I chose set a limit to how late the "trailing edge" (injector turns off) timing could be to ensure the injector would turn off somewhat before the intake valve closes. With my cam I think I chose ~540 degrees as the latest the injector could close - after that point the injector will fire before the exhaust is closed timing I had set. So this rebuild, is it going to be all-out racing or is it still going to be a street motor? The reason I ask is EGR has some positive benefits to a street engine at cruise. EGRs were originally an emissions-only device back in the 70s and early 80s and had to be taken off just to get the engine to run right...and that was right off the showroom floor. But after manufacturers started toying with the EGRs and controlling them with computer precision, they realized there was some positive benefits to having some EGR in the intake mix at most Closed Loop cruise and acceleration conditions. In a round-about way, it acts as an octane booster allowing for more timing...when it's controlled right. At idle and WOT, EGR isn't used so it poses no top-end performance issues at all. response: settings. Ford made quite a few tuned binaries that will run on a given firmware, though... these are just changes to the data region of the firmware, not the actual code region. This is why you're able to run A9L, X3Z, A3M, and various other calibrations on an EEC flashed with GUFB firmware. You will not be able to run, for instance, a CBAZA calibration on a GUFB EEC. No GUFB calibrations going on a PE EEC either. I wouldn't attempt to run a foreign firmware's data on a given EEC. response: as my Injector PWs were above the breakpoint, all was good. But as soon as load was low enough to support PWs bouncing around 2.5ms, everytime adaptive strategy would dip the HEGOs from rich to lean (like normal), it would drop the PW too far due to the excessively steep low-slope value and it was causing bad drivability problems on the down swings of adaptive strategy. I could watch Calcon and see that the engine was hesitating right when adaptive had the HEGOs dipping and the engine would come right back when the HEGOs came back up. So I learned if I'm going to put steep low-slopes in, make sure the breakpoint is lower than what I'll need to drive. Well that didn't help so I just put factory values (19.64/26.1) back in and adjusted things back out using the Backflow correction table & this seems to be working pretty good. I was just hoping there was a more conventional/more appropriate way to do what I was trying to do. garsten wrote: ...lambse1 and 2 are stft's and represent what the eec is commanding for AFR...is this correct?... LAMBSEs are Short-Term Fuel Trims expressed in terms of AFR. And yes, they are what the EEC thinks it is commanding based on MAF Curve, Injector slope...

response: Cobb are ok with stock car but if you've modded intake/exhaust that's what the pro tune is for right? J JamNut 10 posts · Joined 2014 Add to quote #8 · Jan 22, 2015 Yes and no... with aftermarket parts, definitely. But even with a relatively stock vehicle, a professional tune can push your car a little further, taking into account factors like differences in your individual vehicle (e.g. variability in injector flow, fuel pressure regulation, and MAF sensor readings) and environmental factors (like altitude) above/beyond what the stock tune provides. Cars run "open loop" under hard acceleration, there is room for measuring what your individual car is doing and compensating in ways that maximizes output. You can also ask your tuner to push your engine harder or softer than Cobb's off-the-shelf tune, depending on what you want. With factors like ignition timing, you can opt for the safety margin (and associated engine longevity, etc.) that suits your needs. There are also a number of little things they can help you with, like tweaking I, S, S# characteristics (maximum boost, maximum requested torque, max RPM, pedal to throttle response/linearity, etc.) to your liking. So I'm essentially agreeing with what you just said Chris, adding that the reason you got the ping for about 1 second is due to the 1.25 second "LUGTIM" transition from FN901 to FN904A in X3Z. Lugging is correctly defined in A9L as: The strategy provides the capacity of Open Loop Fuel Control during "lugging" conditions ( Part throttle, high Load, low RPM ). FN125 is used to start the lug timer (LUGTMR), but since LDLTM is 5 seconds which is greater than LUGTIM in A9L, open loop cannot be forced through lugging. This was a redundant function anyway since FN320A in combination with FN035 & the open loop delay timers achieve the same goal of forcing open loop under heavy load conditions (unless you've set the load switch to "1' - hehe - it always comes back to this - lol - but forcing open loop while lugging is a definite issue once load scaling is turned off). instruction: Explain boost control in ECU tuning
response: few crank degrees before the intake valve opens. Although you don't want to fire too early or you get too much fuel fired on the valve and thus get fuel pooling on the backside of the valve and that's NOT what you want. Most stock tunes do take advantage of this AFAIK, but most stock tunes have a FAR from zero-overlap cam configuration. Just keep in mind, the larger the injector, the more fuel that gets fired, thus the less time you have before the valve opens to get the fuel on the backside of the valve before pooling begins. The ONLY way that I'm aware of to know when this happens is to try various values and find what runs best. On a sidenote, a "zero-overlap" cam does not mean there is no overlap at all on the cam. All cams have some overlap. It means the overlap is low enough that the intake and exhaust valve are never open at or above .050" at the same time. The E303 using 1.6 ratio rockers represent the highest amount of cam overlap with just BARELY a zero-overlap status. Most cams with durations above 220°@.050" will have some overlap. You can enter cam specs into EA and determine if it is a "zero overlap" cam. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331

Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Oct 01, 2021 10:05 am Displacement is used to calculate a number of things, the main one being Load. Load is a value that represents the amount of air being brought into each cylinder charge relative to the theoretical MAX for natural aspiration. So for a 5.0L V8, each cylinder is capable of holding 0.625L of air (at atmospheric pressure). Using the MAF feedback along with the RPM, the computer can estimate how much air is actually being aspirated into each cylinder fire. The amount relative to the theoretical max is the Load value. I find it amazing how people get 1.8s 1.7s on MT cars. I tried to launch my car at 52 degree weather on Michelin PSS's and all I got was a massive wheel spin , in 1st, 2nd and 3rd gear.It was ridiculuous. So, for those of you that can get into 11s with MT cars, you guys are my heros. By the way, I could consistently get low 12s on my stock turbo FBO AT car on 93 octane with only 370 rwhp. It would just be a test. If you find its doing something differently I'd love to see what that is and then add that functionality to the JB4. I just don't think it's doing anything differently there. So long decels should not have an ongoing transient leanout. Keep in mind that transient enrichment only happens on Change in Load. When the Load goes from 20% to 50%, there's a positive enrichment over a short period of time. When the load drops from 50% to 20%, there's a negative enrichment (what I'm calling enleanment if that's a real word) over a short period of time. But once the decel is sustained, the load should be fairly stable. Depending on the vehicle, a high RPM Closed Throttle Decel should be in the low teens at the highest. There isn't a simple conversion factor to convert load into a boost target, it's much more complicated than that and with good reason. The reason the "modern" BMW turbos engines drive like NA engines rather old school turbo motors is because of the huge amount of code BMW created to control the manifold pressure target. The issue is that when tuners make changes to the stock map they change the wrong tables or only change some of the tables in that mass of logic in an attempt to raise the target manifold pressure. Like you mentioned you have been messing with the BRO table and putting a high figure in the BLM table which. It works in a limited fashion for most tuners but cracks start to emerge when you look closely. What you are seeing is the result of a poor tune which is exasperated by the fudging of the TMAP sensor scaling. Assuming you had a relatively stable throttle position and you were getting these dips, that would suggest some kind of bad connection. Being its happening with multiple MAFs, that would suggest it isn't happening in the MAF. The problem could be from the connector all the way to the inside of the EEC. If I had just bought a $50k+ high end car, I’d probably use premium just out of principle alone. It’s true that premium fuel has less energy than regular, but what’s much more important is that premium fuel has a higher anti-knock index and your car’s engine was designed for premium. There’s really no benefit from using regular in car that was designed for premium. Best case scenerio, you get less power and less fuel economy (since the knock sensors will reduce timing, and the ECU will fatten up the fuel mixture to prevent damage, using more fuel in doing so). instruction: Explain fuel mapping in ECU tuning
response: The Widebands are only required when tuning for OL conditions like WOT where you expect the fuel to be much richer (in the 11:1-13.5:1 ranges) and running lean at WOT (i.e. 14:1) is still richer than what you'd run at Closed Loop (14.5-14.7:1). That doesn't mean they won't be useful at the Closed Loop loads. It's always nice to get a 2 sensor readings (the narrow and wideband readings) to confirm conditions. It just means widebands are not required for tuning for drivability in the closed loop conditions. Make sense??? As for tuning, make sure you get the RT version of the TwEECer. You can't do justice with tuning without getting datalogs of what's happening so you can do deep-level analysis after you've run the car. As well, you'll want to plan on purchasing EEC Analyzer. It will open your datalogs and do much of the mathematical brain-busting stuff for you. It's well worth the money especially to a person new to the tuning world. BTW, welcome to the site. Launch Control Stage 2 Clear RPM (Z_LC_NLM2_CL) - RPM to return to 1/2 fueling once Stage 2 has been entered. Once you've dropped below the Stage 2 activation, the RPMs will drop fast without fuel. So as with Z_LC_NLM1_CL, I say keep this value just below Z_LC_NLM2_SH. The intention is that you bounce between Stage 1 and 2 as fast as possible to maintain a "staging" RPM. The faster you can cut and return fuel, I expect the less RPM hunting that will occur. Although some is inevitable without additional fuel cut stages that cut fuel by more than 1/2 but don't cut it completely. Again, experiment around and find out what works best, and report back. But here's what the GUFB doc has to say: GUFB Doc wrote: Normal Part throttle is (FN904A * FN212A + FN905A * FN129A). During normal part throttle operation, the logic "interpolates" between sea level table (FN904A) and altitude table (FN905A) to calculate base spark. Tip-in Spark (LOM) is (1 - LUGTMR/LUGTIM) * FN901 On accelerating from a standstill, the strategy uses a more aggressive spark table (FN901) for improved performance. Over a period of time (LUGTIM), the spark shifts from LOM spark to normal part throttle spark. The LUGTMR logic is described in the Timer Chapter. This indicates that the Base table should give a little more spark on tip-in from a stand-still to help with performance. So when I read this, I decided to run that table about 2° higher than my Sea/Alt tables to see if it helped any. instruction: Explain turbo lag in ECU tuning
response: explanation why the same condition, being lean, is experienced so differently amongst different people on different builds. Now here's the fixing it part. There are a number of different causes for why you are leaning out. The most common is your MAF curve isn't dialed in well. Thus when you are at idle, the LAMBSEs are settling out to a value that works for idle, but the moment you push on the pedal, the required LAMBSE value to not run lean is much lower. Well older EECs are more reactive than proactive. So they have to see the lean condition then react to it. But while it is reacting, you are experiencing the lean condition. What you want to do is modify the MAF curve so that it reports such that the EEC doesn't have to respond to a lean condition and instead it commands the fuel needed for that condition more accurately. Another common problem is the MAF curve is good, but the initial tip-in just needs a little more juice. On carbs, this was done with accelerator pumps. EECs have a similar concept known as transient fueling. This is where the EEC enriches the mix by some pre-defined amount based on RPM/Load, change in Load (EFTRFF in GUFx EECs) and/or just TPS position and rate...

Keep in mind that if the fuel pump is undersized, raising the fuel pressure isn't going to help. In fact, it's going to do the opposite. Pump flow curves show that a typical pump's flowrate is reduced as pressure increases. The only time increasing fuel pressure should be used to increase fuel delivery is if injectors are maxing out at 90+% duty cycle while at WOT. In these cases, the increased pressure will help overcome injector inadequacy. But the fuel pump has to be capable of delivering the max fuel demand at this elevated pressure. On a N/A engine, that's probably not a big deal, but on a heavily boosted engine where the fuel pump will already be stressed by having to push the rated fuel pressure PLUS your boost pressure, this becomes a recipe for disaster for the pump if it isn't sized to deliver under heavy boost conditions. A lot of people forget that if you are pushing 15 PSI into the intake, the fuel rail pressure is ALSO increased by 15 PSI. So if you go setting the fuel pressure from, say 40 PSI to 50. response: Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: Having startup issues, car starts, pops then dies Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Dec 07, 2009 10:51 am Popping is generally a sign of running lean. Make sure your Injector Slope/BP/Offset parameters are consistent with what a 30lb injector should be (I'd have to look that up myself). But if you are fairly sure what you got is what it should be, here are some things you can do: Verify your fuel pressure is in the 43.5PSI range. Most injectors are rated at 43.5PSI but Ford tends to use 39PSI. So an injector sold as say a 30lb injector@43.5PSI may only be 28s with a stock Ford 39PSI regulator. That could cause things to run a little lean, although generally not right at crank. The EEC does a fairly strong effort to run the engine rich right at crank and then lean it out from there. So if it is running lean right at crank, then that means things are probably VERY lean. But I'd still check fuel pressure and get it in the 43-44 range assuming you have an adjustable FPR. Lower the Injector Slopes. While guessing at Injector Slopes is not something you want to do and rely on for a while, you can trial-n-error some slope values into the tune

Also keep in mind when datalogging KAMs/LTFTs, you don't really read the memory of the EEC to get the table of values. You kind of "catch" them as you pass by certain RPM/loads. Thus, if you never hit 3000RPM at 50% load, then when you map your datalog in EA, you'll see a "hole" in the map where that data wasn't available in your datalog. So when doing MAF tuning, you want as diverse of a log as you can possibly get...from idles, cruising, light/moderate/heavy throttle at as wide of an RPM range as you can get and WOTs from as low in the RPMs as you can get all the way to red-line. I have read many forums and most people smooth out the sharp edges in the TB at the IAC and it helps. I have found what causes mine, it’s the IAC itself. When the IAC is unhooked or the computer shuts it trying to idle the car down low enough, the IAC never closes all the way. You can unhook your MAF and pull the TB 2 MAF tube and put your finger over the IAC hole with it unhooked and it pulls a vacuum on your finger and it idles the engine down lower or kills it. Hey @TMac The tune will absolutely take advantage of modifications on the vehicle. All ecoboosts except the older 3.5 gen 1 engine are speed density. Air density is calculated using pressure and temperature. Intake will not need re-tuning because it's speed density not maf Downpipe does not need wastegate changes because of the closed loop PID controller wastegate system that makes constant corrections from the basemap and then learns those values and stores them in KAM (hence kam reset after changing parts) Charge air cooler upgrades (intercoolers) do not need any changes to take advantage of if you follow the OEM LSPI load model where max allowed engine load is modeled off charge air temp. Cooler charge air means the ecu will allow more engine load. Our tune uses the OEM LSPI load model so when charge temps are cooler the engine allows more air load. response: in the car. Using BE, I made some modifications to the tune. 1. The ACT and ECT share transfer functions so I couldn't change the function for the ACT. I went into the Payload section of the definitions and put in the following equation for address 0x0088 ((X/64/1024/5.12)-1.57)*8. I'm subtracting 1.57 from it cause that was the voltage output at atmospheric. I renamed the Tag to Boost. This seems to give me the correct positive PSI readings from the 3 bar MAP but the vacuum reading are low. Hence the question if anybody knows if this is really a linear output device. 2. I edited the transfer function for the VAT to the one listed in another thread by OneSillyNotch. That seemed to be 20 to 30 degrees low so I've changed that some. I also went into the part throttle spark retard vs vat table and edited those values to reduce retard at temperature. I did the same thing for the WOT spark retard vs VAT table. 3. I reset injector size to 42 pph and reduced cold start cranking time. 4. I've copied the premium spark tables into the regular table and reduced overall timing at high load by several degrees. 5. I let the car sit for half an hour, then went out and it fired up fairly quickly and ran for maybe 30 seconds, probably right when the O2 sensor started reading AFR and adjusting fuel trim. I plugged the MAP sensor in and tried to start it, but it just cranks and cranks with no sign of firing. I unplugged the MAF sensor to see if that was doing something, but it wasn't. I then unplugged the MAP sensor since it ran with that unplugged before, but as expected that didn't matter. response: am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: Why would lambse stay at 0.00 when doing datalog Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Jan 25, 2010 8:51 pm It sounds like the payload isn't getting written to the QH. That would make sense if it were only the RPM and a few others that reside in memory addresses at or below 0xFF. But the QH uses passive datalogging for any payload items in addresses above 0xFF. For those, the QH doesn't need any patch code in the tune. It can datalog those things with the EEC running off the stock tune. So if you are getting 0s for LAMBSE, that's an indication that even the passive payload items aren't working. response: am For me, that was a function of the TFI ignition and different RPM logging payloads. There is RPM and something like "high resolution RPM". If you are logging both, "High resolution RPM" expires at ~4080RPM, so then it switches back to just the RPM payload. For me, it looked like I had a misfire at ~4000 RPM (just as you described), when in fact it was the datalog switching from "high resolution RPM" back to "low resolution RPM". Also, the RPM the TFI reports is just plain jittery/jumpy. I converted to EDIS (High data rate ignition) and the RPM reported in the data log is considerably smoother/less jumpy. '89 Mustang X3Z. instruction: Explain turbo lag in ECU tuning
response: knock sum - NASIOC The ECU has perceived a knock event and responded to it if ANY of the following occur: 1. feedback knock correction decreases 2. fine knock learning for the current load/rpm cell decreases. 3. DAM decreases (other than being reset after a reflash/reset). The problem is that if you are only logging one of the above, then you will not catch a knock event when one of the others is active (based on conditions). Only one of these is active at any given time (i.e. only one will potentially change for a given knock event, if any). Knock sum is incremented with any non-consecutive knock event, regardless of whether or not the ECU responds to it. That means it will increment even at idle and low rpm/load where the ECU chooses not to respond. So, the knock sum value in and of itself is useless. What is useful is watching when it increments (except at low load/rpm). When you see feedback knock correction, decrease in current fine knock learning, or the DAM decreases, you will also see the knock sum increment. That makes the knock sum useful to log in place of the 3 response factors (assuming your ECU supports knock sum). Bill Click to expand... Save Share Like You mentioned...
